Below is a reference on the Dafny language and verifier, followed by your task. === DAFNY REFERENCE === # Dafny reference for verification work Based on the Dafny Reference Manual (https://dafny.org/latest/DafnyRef/DafnyRef). Section numbers in brackets point to the manual. ## 1. How Dafny verifies - Dafny is **modular**: each method and function is verified on its own, using only the *specifications* (not the bodies) of the methods it calls. [13.6.1.3] - A program is verified when every method and function verifies and there are no unproven assumptions (`assume` statements). [13.6.1.3] - Specifications and ghost code are used only during verification; the compiler drops them. [1] - Dafny first checks that each specification is **well-formed** on its own (no out-of-bounds index, null dereference or division by zero inside `requires`/`ensures`), then checks the body against the specification. These are reported as separate assertion batches. [7.8] ## 2. Contracts | Clause | Meaning | Default when absent | |---|---|---| | `requires P` | Precondition. Checked at every call site; the body may assume it on entry. | `requires true` | | `ensures Q` | Postcondition. Must hold on every return path. | `ensures true` | | `modifies S` | Heap locations a method (or loop) may write. | Nothing (empty set) for methods | | `reads S` | Heap locations a function may read. | Functions: nothing. Methods: anything (`*`) | | `decreases E` | Termination measure for recursion or loops. | Dafny guesses (see §4) | [7.1.1–7.1.6] - Multiple `requires` (or `ensures`) clauses are **conjoined in order**. Order matters: an earlier conjunct can make a later one well-defined, e.g. `requires 0 < a.Length` before `requires a[0] == 0`. [7.1.1, 7.1.2] - Clauses can be labeled: `requires L: 0 < i < 10`. [7.1.1] - Framing applies only to the heap (objects and arrays). Local variables, `seq`, `set`, `multiset` and `map` are values and never appear in frames. [7.1.4] - `modifies` means "may write". Writing a location not in the frame is an error even if the old value is restored later. Newly allocated objects may always be modified. [7.1.6] ```dafny class Thermostat { var target: int var history: seq method SetTarget(t: int) modifies this // writes fields of this object ensures target == t ensures history == old(history) + [old(target)] // old(...) = value on entry { history := history + [target]; target := t; } } ``` ## 3. Loops Multiple `invariant` clauses are conjoined in source order. [7.1.7] For a loop `while G invariant I { Body }`, Dafny proves: 1. **I holds on entry**: it must be true just before the loop is first reached. [7.1.7, 8.15.1] 2. **I is maintained**: assuming `I && G` at the start of an iteration, `I` holds again after `Body`. [8.15.1] 3. **After the loop, Dafny knows only `I && !G`** (plus facts about variables the loop does not assign). Anything needed later, such as the method's postcondition, must follow from that. Dafny does not discover loop properties by itself. [8.15.1] Other rules: - Invariants are **not checked at `break`**. [8.15.4] - **Loop targets**: local variables that the loop body never assigns are known to be unchanged. If the body may write the heap, the loop's effective `modifies` clause is the enclosing method's unless the loop declares its own. Add an invariant (or a narrower loop `modifies`) to keep facts about heap locations the loop does not touch. [8.15.3] ```dafny method Clamp(a: array, lo: int, hi: int) requires lo <= hi modifies a ensures forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> lo <= a[k] <= hi ensures forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length && lo <= old(a[k]) <= hi ==> a[k] == old(a[k]) { var i := 0; while i < a.Length invariant 0 <= i <= a.Length // bounds invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i ==> lo <= a[k] <= hi // done part: in range invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i && lo <= old(a[k]) <= hi ==> a[k] == old(a[k]) invariant forall k :: i <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] == old(a[k]) // rest: untouched { if a[i] < lo { a[i] := lo; } else if a[i] > hi { a[i] := hi; } i := i + 1; } // Here Dafny knows: invariants && !(i < a.Length), so i == a.Length. } ``` Checks on this example: - *On entry*: with `i == 0`, the bounds hold and the `0 <= k < 0` invariants are vacuously true; the "untouched" invariant holds because nothing has been written yet. - *Maintained*: the body changes only `a[i]`, so the facts about `k < i` still hold, the new element `a[i]` is now in range (and unchanged if it already was), and the "untouched" invariant still covers `k >= i + 1`. - *After the loop*: `i <= a.Length && !(i < a.Length)` gives `i == a.Length`, so the "done part" invariants become the postconditions. Without the upper bound `i <= a.Length`, this last step fails. Without the "untouched" invariant, the second postcondition fails, because Dafny would not know what `a[i]` held before the iteration that changed it. ## 4. Termination - Every loop and recursive call needs a measure that **strictly decreases** and is **bounded below** (for integers, the bound is 0). [8.15.2] - For a loop guard `i < n`, Dafny guesses `decreases n - i`. For recursion, it guesses the parameter list in order. [8.15.2, 7.1.3] - Measures are lexicographic tuples: `decreases x, y`. [7.1.3] - `decreases *` skips the termination proof (allowed for loops and compiled methods only, not for functions or lemmas); a method calling such code must be `decreases *` too. [7.1.3] - Termination is its own check. It is separate from loop invariants and postconditions. ## 5. Types and collections | Type | Key operations | |---|---| | `int`, `nat` | `nat` is `int` restricted to `0 <= n`. Division and `%` are Euclidean: `a % b` is never negative. No implicit `int`/`real` conversion; use `as int` / `as real`. | | `seq` | `|s|`, `s[i]`, `s[i := v]`, `s + t`, `x in s`, slices `s[lo..hi]`, `s[lo..]`, `s[..hi]`; `s[0..|s|] == s`; `<` / `<=` mean (proper) prefix. | | `set` | `x in s`, `x !in s`, `|s|`, `+` union, `-` difference, `*` intersection, `!!` disjoint. | | `multiset` | `m[x]` multiplicity, `+`, `-`, `*`, `|m|`; `multiset(s)` converts a sequence. | | `map` | `m[k]`, `m[k := v]`, `k in m`, `m.Keys`, `m.Values`, `m.Items`; `+` merges (right side wins). | | `array` | `a.Length`, `a[i]`, `new int[n]`. Arrays live on the heap and need `modifies`/`reads`. `a[..]`, `a[lo..hi]`, `a[lo..]`, `a[..hi]` give a `seq` (requires `0 <= lo <= hi <= a.Length`). | [5.5, 5.6.3.1, 5.10.2] Common idioms: - Permutation of an array: `multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..]))`. - Sortedness: `forall i, j :: 0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]`. - Quantifier bounds also act as well-formedness guards: `forall i :: 0 <= i < |s| ==> s[i] > 0`. ## 6. Two-state expressions - `old(e)`: value of heap reads in `e` on method entry. It has no effect on locals or parameters. `old@L(e)` uses the state at label `L`. [9.22] - `fresh(e)`: objects in `e` were allocated after method entry. [9.23] - `unchanged(o)`: every field of `o` is equal to its value on entry. [9.25] ## 7. Functions, predicates, lemmas and proof statements - **Functions** are pure; the body defines them, so a postcondition is usually not needed. **Predicates** are boolean functions. A `ghost` function or predicate exists only for verification. [6.3, 7.3] - **Lemmas** are ghost methods used as proofs: `lemma L(x: T) requires P(x) ensures Q(x) { ... }`. Calling `L(x)` makes `Q(x)` available. Prefer `requires P ensures Q` over `ensures P ==> Q`. [6.3.3, 13.7.1.3] - `assert P;` makes Dafny prove `P` at that point and then use it. Good for locating where a proof breaks. [8.17] - `assert P by { ... }` proves `P` using the block's steps, then forgets them. [8.17] - `assume P;` is accepted without proof and makes the program unsound; Dafny warns about it. [8.18] - `forall x | P(x) ensures Q(x) { L(x); }` proves `forall x :: P(x) ==> Q(x)` from a lemma. [6.3] - `calc == { A; B; { L(x); } C; }` writes a chain of equalities (or `<`, `<=`, `==>`, ...) with justifications. [8.23, 13.7.1.3] ### Worked proofs **Induction with a lemma.** A recursive lemma call is the induction hypothesis. Dafny checks that the lemma's `decreases` measure (here `n`) goes down. ```dafny function Rep(x: int, n: nat): seq { if n == 0 then [] else [x] + Rep(x, n - 1) } lemma RepLength(x: int, n: nat) ensures |Rep(x, n)| == n { if n > 0 { RepLength(x, n - 1); // induction hypothesis for n - 1 } } ``` **A `calc` proof.** Each step is checked separately; the hint in braces is used for the step it sits on. ```dafny lemma RepAppend(x: int, n: nat, m: nat) ensures Rep(x, n + m) == Rep(x, n) + Rep(x, m) { if n > 0 { calc == { Rep(x, n + m); [x] + Rep(x, (n - 1) + m); // unfold the definition { RepAppend(x, n - 1, m); } // induction hypothesis [x] + (Rep(x, n - 1) + Rep(x, m)); ([x] + Rep(x, n - 1)) + Rep(x, m); // concatenation is associative Rep(x, n) + Rep(x, m); // fold the definition } } } ``` **Using a lemma inside a loop with `assert ... by`.** The lemma's fact is needed only to re-establish the invariant, so it is kept inside the `by` block. ```dafny method Fill(x: int, n: nat) returns (s: seq) ensures s == Rep(x, n) { s := []; var i := 0; while i < n invariant 0 <= i <= n invariant s == Rep(x, i) { s := s + [x]; assert s == Rep(x, i + 1) by { RepAppend(x, i, 1); // Rep(x, i + 1) == Rep(x, i) + Rep(x, 1), and Rep(x, 1) == [x] } i := i + 1; } } ``` **Permutation with `multiset`.** Swapping two elements keeps the multiset of the array, so the permutation invariant is maintained automatically. The invariant `i % 2 == 0` is what lets Dafny conclude, after the loop, that every pair was handled. ```dafny method SwapPairs(a: array) modifies a ensures multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..])) ensures forall k :: 0 <= k && k + 1 < a.Length && k % 2 == 0 ==> a[k] == old(a[k + 1]) && a[k + 1] == old(a[k]) { var i := 0; while i + 1 < a.Length invariant 0 <= i <= a.Length invariant i % 2 == 0 invariant multiset(a[..]) == multiset(old(a[..])) invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < i && k % 2 == 0 ==> a[k] == old(a[k + 1]) && a[k + 1] == old(a[k]) invariant forall k :: i <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] == old(a[k]) { a[i], a[i + 1] := a[i + 1], a[i]; i := i + 2; } } ``` ## 8. Reading verifier output Each error line has the form `file.dfy(line,col): Error: message`. When a specification clause is involved, a `Related location` line points at the clause that could not be proved. Exact wording varies across Dafny versions ("might not hold" in older ones, "could not be proved" in newer ones). | Message | What failed | |---|---| | `a postcondition could not be proved on this return path` + `this is the postcondition that could not be proved` | An `ensures` clause does not follow from the state at that return. | | `this loop invariant could not be proved on entry` | The invariant is false just before the loop. | | `this invariant could not be proved to be maintained by the loop` | One iteration of the body does not re-establish the invariant. | | `a precondition for this call could not be proved` + `this is the precondition that could not be proved` | A callee's `requires` clause is not established at the call. | | `function precondition could not be proved` | A function is applied outside its `requires`. | | `assertion might not hold` / `this proposition could not be proved` | An `assert` (or an internal assertion) cannot be proved. | | `index out of range`, `lower bound out of range`, `upper bound below lower bound or above length of ...` | An index or slice may be out of bounds, possibly inside a specification. | | `decreases expression might not decrease`, `decreases expression must be bounded below by 0`, `this decreases clause was not satisfied` | Termination. | | `value does not satisfy the subset constraints of 'nat'` | A value may be negative where a `nat` is required. | | `possible division by zero` | A divisor may be 0. | Messages such as `arguments to > must be of a numeric type ...` or `first argument to && must be of type bool` are **type errors**, reported before verification. The program must type-check before any of the checks above run. ## 9. Debugging a failing proof The manual's method is to turn the failure into an `assert` and move it backwards (computing the weakest precondition) until the problem is obvious. [13.7.1] 1. **Failing postcondition**: replace `return e;` with `r := e; return;`, then add `assert ;` just before the return. The error moves to the `assert`. 2. **Move the assert up** through statements: | Code after the failing point | Assert before it | |---|---| | `x := Y; assert P;` | `assert P[x := Y];` | | `if B { assert P; ... }` | `assert B ==> P;` | | `if B { ... } else { assert P; ... }` | `assert !B ==> P;` | | `var x := m(k); assert P(x);` (with `m` requires `A`, ensures `B`) | `assert A(k); assert forall x :: B(k, x) ==> P(x);` | 3. **Split** compound goals: `assert A && B;` into `assert A; assert B;`, and `assert A ==> B;` into `if A { assert B; }`. 4. **Quantifiers**: prove `forall x :: P(x) ==> Q(x)` with `forall x | P(x) ensures Q(x) { assert Q(x); }`. For `exists`, assert the property for a concrete witness first: `assert P(x0);`. 5. **For loops**, check the three obligations in §3 separately: assert the invariant just before the loop, assert it at the end of the body, and assert the postcondition right after the loop. [13.7.1.1–13.7.1.3] **Counterexamples**: `--extract-counterexample` reports a possible counterexample as a set of assumptions about variable values. Dafny cannot guarantee that it actually violates the assertion, so treat it as a hint. [13.7.1.4] ## 10. Command line ``` dafny verify program.dfy dafny verify --extract-counterexample program.dfy # report a potential counterexample dafny verify --verification-time-limit 30 program.dfy # seconds per verification attempt dafny verify --isolate-assertions program.dfy # verify each assertion in its own batch ``` [13.6.1.3, 13.9.7] For slow or timing-out proofs: `assume false;` at a point stops verification there, which helps find the expensive part (remove it afterwards). `assert P by { ... }` keeps helper facts from slowing down later proofs. [13.7.2] === END OF DAFNY REFERENCE === You are a formal verification assistant.
